body_markdown:
The big to-do of the Specialty Equipment Marketing Association (SEMA) is in full swing right now in Las Vegas, where custom builders and manufacturers are showing off their wildest creations, each synergistically aligned with bleeding-edge parts from established and upstart suppliers alike. You may have seen[a SEMA story](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/sema/) or two on the site this week…


All that customizing got us thinking about the money-no-object, skills aplenty builds we’d love to show off at SEMA if given the chance. Here’s what we came up with. What would you dream up and build to debut at SEMA?


## Franco-American Perfection


Wikimedia Commons/Kilyann Le Hen


I’d shoehorn the 472-horse twin-turbo LF4 V-6 from the baby Cadillac Blackwing into the back of an early 1990s Alpine GTA Le Mans. This adorable oddball Renault doesn’t get the same attention as its gorgeous predecessor, the rally-conquering Alpine A110—nor should it, really—but it is really cool in its own right. Only 325 Le Mans models were made, and I don’t think there’s much to be done to improve upon the body, so I’d focus on yoinking the anemic Renault V-6 (the same Peugeot-Renault-Volvo engine no one loves in any application), tweaking the suspension, and improving the surfaces on the interior. — *Eddy Eckart*


## Hot Hudson


Hudson


My understanding as to the point of a SEMA build is to get people talking about it and the companies whose parts were used on it. I doubt many cars would get people talking quite like a 1948 Hudson Commodore.


The step-down Hudsons are a ripe blank slate to build something cool. There is plenty of space inside, and though I’m sure the wheel and tire people won’t love the skirted rear fenders, the whole car is sleek in a way that many of the popular models used for builds just aren’t. Fully restored or wearing patina, a well-done Hudson could steal the show. — *Kyle Smith*


## A Lincoln for the Kids


1939 Lincoln K LeBaron Coupe


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


I keep hearing that younger enthusiasts have zero interest in prewar cars, so I’m going to get a little bit funky with this pick and see if maybe doing something wildly unexpected with one of those cars would zag so hard the youths would appreciate it.


Let’s go with a Lincoln K Series, and we’ll drop it as low as possible on some kind of wild air suspension system. The picture here is a 1939 Lincoln K LeBaron coupe, and I think it would look wild with some flashy wheels and a new ride height. Does that equate to looking good? Listen, I never said that. But I’d bet it would get people talking. — *Nathan Petroelje*


## Of Two Minds…


A long-tail Prius land-speed racer would be pretty funny, I think. — *Grace Jarvis, yesterday*


Josh Sweeney


Forget my land-speed-racer Prius idea (wouldn’t it look sweet with a long tail?). I’m gonna jump on the prewar wagon and advocate for a land-speed Model T instead. A whole flock of these exists, as Kyle Smith discovered when he attended the[Montana 500](https://www.hagerty.com/media/great-reads/montana-500-model-ts-doing-the-impossible-since-1961/) , but they are painstakingly period-correct. Indeed, cars wearing updated parts or modernized systems are disqualified from the event. This appears to be an opportunity. What if you asked one of these speedy T aficionados to build the most illegal T possible for the Montana 500? We could loosen up the timeframe for “aftermarket parts” a good bit, to perhaps 1945. I am absolutely sure they would not want anything to do with this silly project, but I’m having fun thinking about it. Imagine commissioning someone to build a magnesium version of the T’s wooden wheels! — *Grace Jarvis, today*


## eMack


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


I like big trucks, and I cannot lie. Furthermore, I have always loved the look of the streamlined Mack B-series, with their rounded edges and integrated headlights. Built from 1953 to ’66, they were a sweet spot of tractor design. I think a single-axle B-61, low and mean but also updated with the electric powertrain out of a Freightliner eCascadia or Volvo F-series, would be killer. Paint the thing dark purple and put it on some giant Alcoa wheels (maybe polished, maybe black) with fat tires. Stick a carbon fiber bulldog on the nose and blast the screeching, roaring soundtrack of[Darth Vader’s Tie Advanced X1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eBN8H2BHFO0) out of the stack. That seems like a pretty slick, SEMA-appropriate build to me. — *Stefan Lombard*
